Trilinear interpolation is the direct 3D extension of bilinear interpolation, defined as the linear interpolation of two bilinear interpolations [S15, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly describes the implementation of trilinear interpolation in the `interpolate` function. The code calculates intermediate values `c00`, `c01`, `c10`, and `c11` by performing linear interpolation along the X-axis (e.g., `c00 = c000*(1-xd) + c100*xd`). These intermediate values represent bilinear interpolations in the XY plane (or planes parallel to it). Subsequently, the code performs linear interpolation along the Y-axis (`c0 = c00*(1-yd) + c10*yd`) and then along the Z-axis (`c = c0*(1-zd) + c1*zd`). This step-by-step process—interpolating along one axis to get results that are then interpolated along the next, and so on—is mathematically equivalent to the linear interpolation of two bilinear interpolations (specifically, interpolating the results of bilinear interpolations on the front and back faces of the voxel along the depth axis). Thus, the evidence supports the claim that the method is defined as the linear interpolation of two bilinear interpolations.
